ENT Clinical Note

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • 1-week history of sore throat followed by dry cough; no specific trigger identified.

- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Sore throat began Thu/Fri last week.  
  • Dry, non-productive cough started 1–2 days later (Sat/Sun).  
  • Shortness of breath developed 3–4 days ago, mainly on exertion; no limitation of basic activities, but “unusual” for patient.  
  • Intermittent low-grade fever during first 3 days; now resolved.  
  • Symptoms fluctuate day-to-day; no sustained improvement yet.

- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat: persistent soreness; no reported throat-closing sensation, dysphagia, odynophagia, drooling, or voice change.  
  • Nasal/ocular: denies congestion; no rhinorrhea, sneezing, or eye symptoms.  
  • Airway/respiratory: exertional dyspnea; denies stridor or noisy breathing.  
  • Swelling: no lip, tongue, uvular, or facial swelling.  
  • Ear/neck: no otalgia, hearing change, neck pain, or palpable neck lumps per self-exam.  
  • Chest: describes mild wheeze and occasional chest pain.

- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • No prior similar respiratory/ENT episodes and no prior hospital care for airway issues.

- Allergies and current medications:
  • Allergy: peanuts (reaction details not discussed).  
  • Current medications: none.  
  • Over-the-counter use: paracetamol advised but not yet started (dose/route/frequency not documented).

- Social context:
  • Adult patient (DOB 09 May 2016 given; likely erroneous, but recorded as stated). Lives in UK, able to perform daily activities, currently off work; requests sick note.

Objective:
- Observable swelling and distribution: Not reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors: Patient reports exertional dyspnea and self-described wheeze; no observed stridor.
- Mental status/associated features: Headaches come and go; denies dizziness or syncope.
- Vitals and physical examination: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with patient: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Probable viral upper respiratory tract infection with associated dry cough and mild exertional dyspnea.
- No clinical features to suggest acute epiglottitis, peritonsillar abscess, or anaphylaxis at present.
- Risk factors for serious lower respiratory pathology (e.g., TB, malignancy) low; symptoms expected to be self-limiting.
- Peanut allergy noted but not relevant to current presentation.

Plan:
- Immediate actions/advice:
  • Symptomatic management: paracetamol for pain/fever, adequate oral hydration, rest.  
  • No antibiotics indicated at this time.

- Specific instructions:
  • If breathlessness worsens, becomes sudden or severe, or if new red-flag symptoms appear (stridor, voice change, difficulty swallowing, swelling, high fever, hemoptysis), seek urgent in-person medical review or emergency services.  
  • Return for assessment if symptoms persist beyond 4–5 days or deteriorate.

- Sick note:
  • Doctor to provide certificate for additional days off work (duration per clinician discretion).

- Follow-up:
  • Arrange routine GP/ENT review if no improvement or if red flags develop.  
  • Reinforce avoidance of peanut exposure; consider discussing self-management plan and auto-injector at future visit (not performed today).

Quality checks:
● Missing expected elements:
  – Objective vital signs (temperature, HR, RR, SpO₂).  
  – Direct visualization of oropharynx/tonsils, neck palpation, lung auscultation.  
  – Detailed description of peanut allergy reaction history and availability of epinephrine auto-injector.

● Internal conflicts:
  – Patient initially denied shortness of breath then affirmed it; conflict noted.

● Transcript quality:
  – Generally clear; minor interruptions and one likely date-of-birth error (2016) noted.
